case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal courts have jurisdiction under 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(D) to review an immigration judge/BIA determination that a noncitizen failed to show the “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” required for cancellation of removal—i.e., whether applying that statutory hardship standard to established facts is a reviewable “question of law.”
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(D) (restoring jurisdiction for “constitutional claims or questions of law” despite other jurisdiction-stripping provisions), in interaction with the cancellation-of-removal hardship criterion (8 U.S.C. § 1229b(b)(1)(D)) and related limits on review in 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(B).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues the hardship eligibility inquiry for non-LPR cancellation of removal is a mixed question of law and fact because it requires applying a statutory legal standard (“exceptional and extremely unusual hardship”) to established facts; under Guerrero-Lasprilla, such mixed questions fall within “questions of law” in § 1252(a)(2)(D), so courts of appeals may review whether the agency correctly applied the hardship standard (while still not reweighing evidence or revisiting pure factfinding). Petitioner and supporting amici emphasize that a contrary rule invites inconsistent outcomes, turns jurisdiction on artful characterization of issues, and deprives vulnerable applicants (including domestic-violence survivors) of meaningful judicial review of legal errors in hardship analyses that often determine whether deportation occurs.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues that the hardship determination is essentially a discretionary, highly fact-intensive judgment call insulated from judicial review by the INA’s jurisdiction-stripping scheme; permitting review would, in practice, convert unreviewable factual and discretionary determinations into reviewable legal questions and entangle courts in reweighing evidence and second-guessing the agency’s case-by-case hardship assessments. The government’s approach treats hardship determinations as outside § 1252(a)(2)(D)’s “questions of law” exception (except perhaps for purely legal issues such as the articulation of the standard), and maintains that courts lack jurisdiction over challenges that are, at bottom, disagreements with the agency’s evaluation of the facts and degree of hardship.
key_precedents: Ray Haluch Gravel Co. v. Central Pension Fund, 571 U.S. 177 (2014)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas are right that hardship is degree-laden and that review can easily slide into reweighing evidence—precisely what § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i) and Patel prohibit. But that pragmatic concern cannot erase § 1252(a)(2)(D)’s “notwithstanding” restoration of jurisdiction for “questions of law,” and Guerrero-Lasprilla’s holding that this includes application of a legal standard to established facts; the narrower, institutionally sound line is to allow review only for legal misapplication of the hardship framework while forbidding relitigation of factfinding or discretionary weighing. Patel, properly read, reinforces that boundary by insulating factual determinations and discretionary judgments, not by nullifying Congress’s express carveout for legal error. I would therefore keep jurisdiction tightly cabined to whether the agency used the correct legal yardstick on the facts it found, as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett suggest, which addresses the floodgates concern without making § 1252(a)(2)(D) a dead letter.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed “cabined” review—legal misapplication only—cannot be squared with the text Congress chose in § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i), which bars review of “any judgment regarding the granting of relief” under § 1229b; the hardship call is itself a quintessential eligibility judgment and not a separable, rule-like legal question. Guerrero-Lasprilla does not compel jurisdiction here because the “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” standard is an evaluative, degree-laden determination whose so-called “application” inevitably entails reassessing the significance of facts, thereby collapsing § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i) into § 1252(a)(2)(D). Patel strengthens, rather than weakens, this reading by emphasizing Congress’s sweeping foreclosure of review in discretionary-relief regimes, and § 1252(a)(2)(D) is best read—consistent with that structure—to preserve review for genuine legal errors (wrong standard, categorical rule, legally forbidden factor), not case-specific sufficiency disputes masquerading as “mixed questions,” as Justice Alito similarly observes. Under an original public meaning approach, the Court should not create a judge-made jurisdictional middle ground that invites relabeling factual disagreements as “law” and defeats Congress’s jurisdiction-stripping design.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed “cabined” review under § 1252(a)(2)(D), grounded in Guerrero-Lasprilla, is the strongest counter: it seeks to allow only legal misapplication review while barring fact relitigation. But in my view that line is not administrable in this particular statutory context because the “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” inquiry is itself a quintessential degree judgment; calling disagreement about whether found facts meet that vague threshold a “legal” error will inevitably invite the reweighing Patel says Congress foreclosed when it barred review of “any judgment regarding the granting of relief” under § 1229b. Guerrero-Lasprilla involved a more determinate equitable-tolling diligence inquiry, whereas hardship determinations are open-ended and evaluative, so extending mixed-question review here risks swallowing the jurisdictional bar in practice. I would read § 1252(a)(2)(D) narrowly to preserve review for truly legal defects—wrong standard, categorical misrule, failure to consider a legally required factor—without opening the door to appellate second-guessing of hardship sufficiency.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas raise the strongest concern: that hardship review is so degree-laden it will inevitably become forbidden reweighing of evidence, effectively swallowing § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i). But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 1252(a)(2)(D) is a “notwithstanding” carveout, and Guerrero-Lasprilla squarely treats application of a legal standard to established facts as a reviewable question of law—so we cannot erase that jurisdiction simply because it is hard to administer. Patel matters in the way Justice Roberts frames it: it reinforces the boundary by barring review of factfinding and credibility/weight determinations, but it does not authorize insulating legal misapplications of the hardship standard where Congress preserved review. A cabined rule—accepting the agency’s facts while correcting wrong yardsticks, categorical exclusions of legally relevant factors, or legally mistaken understandings of hardship—protects vulnerable families from uncorrectable legal error without turning courts into super-IJs.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas have the best practical point: the hardship inquiry is degree-laden and appellate review can easily become impermissible reweighing of evidence, which § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i) and Patel caution against. But the statutory text of § 1252(a)(2)(D) is a “notwithstanding” restoration of jurisdiction for “questions of law,” and under Guerrero-Lasprilla that includes mixed questions—application of a legal standard to established facts—so we cannot construe (D) down to only ‘pure law’ without effectively overruling that precedent and draining the carveout of meaning. Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed line is the pragmatic, textually coherent reconciliation: review exists for legal misapplication of the hardship standard (wrong yardstick, failure to consider legally required factors, treating irrelevant considerations as dispositive) while Patel continues to bar challenges that dispute factfinding, credibility, or the agency’s weighing of hardship. Under my methodology, that cabined rule both honors Congress’s jurisdiction-stripping choice in (B) and gives operative effect to Congress’s express preservation in (D), addressing floodgates by policing the fact/law boundary rather than collapsing it.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas are right that hardship is degree-laden and that courts must not reweigh evidence under the guise of “review,” especially in light of § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i) and Patel’s emphasis on insulating factual determinations and discretionary judgments. But § 1252(a)(2)(D)’s “notwithstanding” clause restores jurisdiction for “questions of law,” and Guerrero-Lasprilla holds that phrase includes applying a legal standard to established facts; as a textualist, I cannot read that carveout down to near-nothing simply because line-drawing is hard. The harmonizing rule Chief Justice Roberts proposes—accept the agency’s factfinding as conclusive and review only for legal misapplication of the hardship standard (wrong yardstick, legally forbidden categorical rules, failure to consider legally required factors)—gives effect to both provisions without converting courts of appeals into super-IJs. Patel still does real work here by foreclosing any attack on what the facts are or how the agency weighed them; it does not authorize us to nullify Congress’s express preservation of legal-question review.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that hardship is so degree-laden that “application” review will inevitably become forbidden reweighing—carries real practical force, and Patel underscores Congress’s intent to insulate factual findings and discretionary judgments. But Guerrero-Lasprilla is controlling on the meaning of § 1252(a)(2)(D): “questions of law” includes mixed questions applying a legal standard to established facts, and we should not narrow that carveout into near-nullity. As Chief Justice Roberts suggests, the administrable, institutionally modest line is to allow review only for legal error in the framework (wrong yardstick, categorical misrule, failure to consider legally required factors) while taking the agency’s factfinding and weighting as given, which preserves both Patel’s fact/law boundary and Congress’s express notwithstanding clause. Under my precedent- and institution-focused approach, that narrow legal-error check best harmonizes the statutes and avoids making § 1252(a)(2)(D) surplusage.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas press the best argument on their side: that hardship is so degree-laden that “application” review will collapse into impermissible reweighing, effectively swallowing § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i)’s bar on reviewing “any judgment regarding the granting of relief.” But the text of § 1252(a)(2)(D)—especially its “notwithstanding” clause—restores jurisdiction for “questions of law,” and Guerrero-Lasprilla’s ordinary-meaning construction squarely includes applying a legal standard to established facts, so we cannot rewrite that carveout to cover only ‘pure’ legal questions. Patel strengthens, rather than defeats, the line: it underscores that courts may not revisit factfinding, credibility, or evidentiary weight, but it does not authorize insulating legal misapplication of the hardship standard from any review where Congress expressly preserved it. Chief Justice Roberts’s cabined framing is administrable and faithful to the statute’s original public meaning: jurisdiction exists to correct legal misapplication on the agency-found facts, not to conduct de novo hardship balancing.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—echoed by Justice Thomas—is the pragmatic worry that “application” review of hardship will collapse into reweighing evidence and thus defeat § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i). But that concern cannot override § 1252(a)(2)(D)’s express notwithstanding carveout, and Guerrero-Lasprilla’s construction that “questions of law” include applying a legal standard to established facts; the proper response is Chief Justice Roberts’s boundary-policing approach: courts accept agency factfinding as fixed (as Patel requires) and review only for legal misapplication (wrong yardstick, failure to consider legally required factors, or reliance on an impermissible rule). Under my procedural-fairness lens, insulating those legal errors would create a system where removal turns on unreviewable misreadings of the statute, while a cabined legal-error review preserves uniformity without converting courts into super-IJs. Patel narrows the inquiry by barring review of factual disputes and discretionary weighing, but it does not authorize reading (D) into near-surplusage in this context.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(D) restores jurisdiction for “questions of law,” and Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr holds that this phrase includes mixed questions—i.e., applying a statutory legal standard to undisputed or established facts. The hardship inquiry under § 1229b(b)(1)(D) fits that description when the facts are taken as found and the only issue is whether they satisfy the statutory threshold, while § 1252(a)(2)(B) and Patel v. Garland still foreclose review of underlying factfinding and discretionary weighing of evidence. A narrow ruling recognizing jurisdiction only for the legal application of the hardship standard (not for reweighing facts) respects Congress’s jurisdiction-stripping scheme, adheres to precedent, and promotes uniformity and institutional legitimacy by ensuring legal standards are applied consistently.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of § 1252(a)(2)(D) restores jurisdiction only for “constitutional claims or questions of law,” and the “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” inquiry in § 1229b(b)(1)(D) is a quintessentially fact-bound, discretionary eligibility judgment that Congress insulated from review through § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i). Although Guerrero-Lasprilla read “questions of law” to include some applications of law to established facts, that construction should not be extended to transform the INA’s jurisdiction-stripping scheme into broad review of hardship determinations, which in practice would require reweighing evidence and second-guessing the agency’s assessment. Patel v. Garland confirms that Congress used sweeping language to preclude review of judgments “regarding the granting of relief,” and the better textual reading harmonizes § 1252(a)(2)(D) as preserving review of pure legal errors (e.g., the wrong legal standard), not the agency’s application of a vague hardship standard to particular facts.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(B) broadly strips jurisdiction over “any judgment regarding the granting of relief” under § 1229b, and the hardship inquiry in § 1229b(b)(1)(D) is quintessentially a case-specific, fact-intensive judgment about degree rather than a legal issue susceptible to appellate correction. Although § 1252(a)(2)(D) preserves review for “constitutional claims or questions of law,” Patel v. Garland emphasizes the INA’s sharp fact/law distinction and cautions against using § 1252(a)(2)(D) to repackage unreviewable factual determinations as legal questions. Guerrero-Lasprilla’s allowance for some mixed questions does not require jurisdiction here because reviewing “application” of the hardship standard would, in practice, invite courts to reweigh evidence and second-guess the agency’s discretionary assessment—precisely what § 1252(a)(2)(B) was designed to prevent. The better reading is that courts may review only purely legal questions (e.g., the correct articulation of the hardship standard), not whether the established facts satisfy it.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(D) expressly restores jurisdiction over “constitutional claims or questions of law” notwithstanding the jurisdiction-stripping provisions in § 1252(a)(2)(B), and Guerrero-Lasprilla holds that “questions of law” include mixed questions—i.e., applying a legal standard to established facts. Determining whether the facts found by the IJ/BIA satisfy the statutory hardship standard in § 1229b(b)(1)(D) is therefore reviewable for legal error (misapplication of the standard or use of an impermissible rule), even if courts may not revisit underlying factfinding or reweigh evidence. Patel confirms the statute draws a fact/law line and bars review of factual determinations, but it does not authorize insulating the agency’s application of a statutory legal standard from any judicial check where Congress preserved review in § 1252(a)(2)(D). Preserving limited review here promotes fairness and guards against arbitrary, inconsistent hardship applications that disproportionately burden U.S.-citizen family members and other vulnerable people affected by removal decisions.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(D) restores jurisdiction for “questions of law” notwithstanding the jurisdiction-stripping provisions, and Guerrero-Lasprilla held that this phrase includes mixed questions—i.e., the application of a legal standard to undisputed or established facts. The “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” requirement in § 1229b(b)(1)(D) is a statutory standard, so reviewing whether the agency correctly applied that standard to the facts fits comfortably within Guerrero-Lasprilla’s understanding of a reviewable question of law, while still leaving Patel and § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i) to bar review of pure factfinding or discretionary reweighing. A workable middle ground is to permit review for legal misapplication (including use of the wrong legal yardstick or failure to consider legally required factors) but not to reopen evidentiary disputes. That approach respects Congress’s limits on review, preserves meaningful correction of legal error, and maintains coherence between § 1252(a)(2)(B) and § 1252(a)(2)(D).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(D) restores jurisdiction for “questions of law,” and its plain meaning, as construed in Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr, includes “the application of a legal standard to undisputed or established facts,” i.e., mixed questions. Applying the statutory phrase “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” in § 1229b(b)(1)(D) to found facts is therefore reviewable as a legal question, even if § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i) otherwise bars review of discretionary cancellation determinations. Patel v. Garland does not compel a different result because it addressed the jurisdictional bar for factual findings underlying eligibility, not § 1252(a)(2)(D)’s express carveout for legal (including mixed) questions; courts may review legal misapplication without reweighing evidence or revisiting pure factfinding. This reading respects Congress’s chosen text and preserves separation-of-powers limits by ensuring agencies remain bound by statutory standards subject to judicial correction when misapplied.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(D) expressly restores jurisdiction for “constitutional claims or questions of law” notwithstanding § 1252(a)(2)(B)’s jurisdiction-stripping, and under Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr that phrase includes mixed questions involving the application of a legal standard to established facts. The cancellation-of-removal hardship criterion in § 1229b(b)(1)(D)—“exceptional and extremely unusual hardship”—is a statutory legal standard, so a court of appeals may review whether the IJ/BIA correctly applied that standard to the found facts, while still lacking jurisdiction to revisit underlying factfinding or reweigh evidence. Patel v. Garland confirms the fact/law line and bars review of pure factual determinations in discretionary-relief proceedings, but it does not displace Guerrero-Lasprilla’s holding that applying a legal standard to settled facts is a reviewable “question of law” under § 1252(a)(2)(D). A limited, law-focused review rule is also more workable and legitimacy-preserving because it gives effect to Congress’s explicit carveout while maintaining judicial restraint from second-guessing case-specific evidentiary judgments.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(D) restores jurisdiction for “questions of law” notwithstanding § 1252(a)(2)(B)’s bar on review of certain discretionary relief decisions, and the ordinary public meaning of “questions of law” encompasses applying a legal standard to established facts. Guerrero-Lasprilla held categorically that this phrase includes such mixed questions, and the hardship inquiry under § 1229b(b)(1)(D)—whether established facts meet the statutory standard of “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship”—fits that description. Patel confirms that § 1252(a)(2)(B) precludes review of underlying factual findings in discretionary-relief proceedings, but it does not negate § 1252(a)(2)(D)’s express carveout for legal questions, which can be honored without reweighing evidence. Courts therefore may review whether the agency applied the correct hardship standard to the facts found, while remaining barred from revisiting factfinding or second-guessing discretionary weighing.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(D) expressly restores jurisdiction over “constitutional claims or questions of law” notwithstanding § 1252(a)(2)(B)’s bar on review of cancellation determinations, and Guerrero-Lasprilla holds that “questions of law” include mixed questions involving application of a legal standard to established facts. Determining whether found facts satisfy the statutory hardship threshold in § 1229b(b)(1)(D) is precisely that kind of application-of-law inquiry, so courts may review whether the agency applied the correct legal framework without reweighing evidence or revisiting pure factfinding. Patel confirms the statute draws a fact/law line—precluding review of factual findings—but does not eliminate § 1252(a)(2)(D) review of legal errors embedded in eligibility determinations. Allowing limited review promotes procedural fairness and guards against inconsistent, uncorrected legal misapplications in high-stakes removal cases while preserving the agency’s discretion over ultimate relief.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(D)’s preservation of review for “questions of law” permits federal courts to review an immigration judge’s/BIA’s application of the “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” standard for cancellation of removal to established facts (i.e., a mixed question of law and fact).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(D) (restoring jurisdiction for “constitutional claims or questions of law” notwithstanding other jurisdiction-stripping provisions, in the context of cancellation of removal hardship determinations under 8 U.S.C. § 1229b).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that the Third Circuit wrongly treated the hardship eligibility determination for cancellation of removal as categorically unreviewable, even when the challenge is that the agency misapplied the governing legal standard to established facts. Relying on Guerrero-Lasprilla, petitioner contends that applying a legal standard to settled facts is itself a “question of law” within § 1252(a)(2)(D), so courts of appeals retain jurisdiction to correct legal errors in hardship adjudications. Petitioner and amici emphasize that insulating hardship determinations from review invites inconsistency, undermines uniformity, and is especially harmful in high-stakes cases (including those involving domestic-violence survivors) where hardship is often dispositive.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues that the “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” assessment is too fact-bound, discretionary, and judgment-laden to qualify as a reviewable “question of law” under § 1252(a)(2)(D). On this view, even if Guerrero-Lasprilla allows review of some mixed questions, hardship determinations in cancellation of removal should fall on the unreviewable side of the line because they effectively involve reweighing facts and second-guessing the agency’s judgment rather than resolving legal questions.
key_precedents: Ray Haluch Gravel Co. v. Central Pension Fund, 571 U.S. 177 (2014)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability objection is the strongest point for Respondent: hardship determinations are evaluative and fact-heavy, and review risks becoming forbidden reweighing that would undercut Congress’s jurisdiction-stripping design. But that concern cannot justify a categorical bar in the face of § 1252(a)(2)(D)’s express restoration for “questions of law,” and Guerrero-Lasprilla’s construction supplies a workable constraint—courts may review only claimed misapplications of the hardship standard to facts as found, not revisit credibility, factfinding, or evidentiary weight. Patel, as Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh stress, is best read to police that boundary against factual end-runs rather than to retract Guerrero-Lasprilla’s mixed-question rule, and we can reinforce institutional legitimacy by emphasizing dismissal of any petition that merely disputes the agency’s weighing. I therefore remain with Petitioner on a narrow ground that preserves limited legal-error review while respecting Congress’s bar on factual and discretionary second-guessing.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern is the strongest point for the respondent, but it asks us to narrow § 1252(a)(2)(D) based on predicted spillover rather than the enacted text restoring jurisdiction for “questions of law.” As the Chief Justice explains, Guerrero-Lasprilla’s construction of that phrase to include applying a legal standard to established facts supplies a workable, text-based limit: courts may correct misapplication of the hardship standard while refusing to revisit factfinding or evidentiary weight. Patel, properly read, reinforces that boundary by foreclosing review of factual determinations and discretionary judgments; it does not authorize a categorical carveout for hardship applications when Congress did not write one. Under an original public meaning approach, the remedy for workload concerns lies with Congress, not judicial revision of the jurisdictional carve-out.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Barrett argue that Guerrero-Lasprilla supplies a manageable limiting principle—reviewing only the application of the hardship standard to “established facts” while barring any reweighing—but I remain skeptical that this is workable in the § 1229b(b)(1)(D) context. Unlike the objective diligence inquiry in Guerrero-Lasprilla, “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” is inherently comparative and evaluative, so deciding whether the agency “misapplied” that standard to a particular family’s circumstances will almost always require a court to reassess the degree and cumulative significance of those circumstances, which Patel warned cannot be repackaged as a legal question. I agree there is jurisdiction under § 1252(a)(2)(D) for genuine legal errors (wrong standard, categorical refusal to consider a legally relevant factor), but recognizing broader as-applied hardship review will predictably expand into routine appellate second-guessing and undercut Congress’s jurisdiction-stripping design. Guerrero-Lasprilla therefore does not, in my view, compel jurisdiction over this kind of fact-saturated hardship application, and Patel’s functional boundary remains the better guide.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern—that hardship review will inevitably become appellate reweighing—deserves respect, but it cannot justify reading § 1252(a)(2)(D) as if it contained an unwritten carveout for hardship applications. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, Guerrero-Lasprilla gives us a workable limiting principle: courts may review only the application of the hardship standard to facts the agency found, while Patel bars relitigating what those facts are or how credible the evidence was. I agree with Justice Alito that “true legal mistakes” remain reviewable, and that is exactly why a narrow mixed-question jurisdiction is necessary—to correct misapplication of the governing standard without turning courts into super-IJs. Given the profound consequences of removal for families, preserving this constrained legal-error review promotes uniformity and basic fairness while still honoring Congress’s channeling of discretionary, fact-bound judgments away from Article III courts.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability warning is the best objection, but it can’t justify reading an atextual exception into § 1252(a)(2)(D): Congress restored jurisdiction over “questions of law,” and Guerrero-Lasprilla’s construction of that phrase as including application of a legal standard to established facts directly covers at least some hardship-as-applied claims. The Chief Justice’s proposed limiting principle is the pragmatic, text-faithful way to honor Patel’s boundary: courts may correct misstatements of the hardship rule, failures to consider legally required factors, or legally erroneous application to the facts as found, while refusing any invitation to revisit what the facts are or to reweigh their significance. Alito is right that hardship is more evaluative than diligence, but our job is to police the characterization of the claim, not to carve out an entire statutory standard from § 1252(a)(2)(D) based on predicted workload. On this reading, we preserve statutory coherence between Guerrero-Lasprilla and Patel and give courts an administrable gatekeeping role rather than an open-ended license to second-guess discretionary judgments.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern is serious, but it cannot supply atextual limits on § 1252(a)(2)(D), which restores jurisdiction for “questions of law” and, under Guerrero-Lasprilla, includes mixed questions applying a legal standard to settled facts. As the Chief Justice notes, the workable limiting principle is to accept the agency’s factfinding and review only whether the “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” standard was legally misapplied; Patel then does its job by foreclosing review of factual disputes and credibility/weighting quarrels. Justice Alito is right that courts must police end-runs, but the answer is disciplined characterization (dismissing repackaged fact challenges), not carving hardship applications out of § 1252(a)(2)(D) without textual warrant. On a separation-of-powers view, we enforce the jurisdictional line Congress wrote—and the line Congress wrote leaves room for genuine legal-error correction even in fact-intensive settings.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability objection has real force—hardship is evaluative and courts could be tempted to reweigh equities—but that concern cannot justify carving hardship applications out of § 1252(a)(2)(D) given Guerrero-Lasprilla’s settled construction that “questions of law” include applying a legal standard to established facts. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, the way to honor Congress’s jurisdiction-stripping design (and Patel’s warning against end-runs) is to enforce a bright boundary: no review of factfinding, credibility, or the weight/cumulative significance the agency assigns; only review for using the wrong legal rule or misapplying the hardship standard to the facts as found. Alito’s attempt to distinguish Guerrero-Lasprilla as “objective” versus “open-ended” is not a text-based limitation in § 1252(a)(2)(D), and institutionally we should prefer a narrow, precedent-consistent rule over an atextual exception driven by workload predictions. Under my precedent- and stability-oriented methodology, a disciplined standard of review addresses the practical risk without rewriting the statutory carve-out Congress enacted.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability objection is serious, but under a textualist approach it cannot displace Congress’s express carveout in § 1252(a)(2)(D), which turns on the character of the claim (“constitutional claims or questions of law”), not the expected ease of application. As the Chief Justice explains, Guerrero-Lasprilla squarely interprets “questions of law” to include mixed questions applying a legal standard to established facts, and nothing in Patel retracts that holding; Patel instead reinforces the separate bar on reviewing factfinding and credibility determinations. The proper answer to Alito’s end-run concern is a jurisdictional gatekeeping rule: accept the agency’s facts and review only whether the hardship standard was misapplied or a legally required factor was ignored, while dismissing any petition that functionally asks for reweighing. On that reading, hardship determinations are not categorically insulated from § 1252(a)(2)(D), and precedent plus the enacted text keep review both limited and legitimate.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern is the hardest issue: hardship is undeniably evaluative, and we should not invite courts of appeals to relitigate the cumulative weight of family circumstances under the guise of “law.” But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, § 1252(a)(2)(D) and Guerrero-Lasprilla provide a workable, disciplined line—accept the agency’s factfindings and review only whether those settled facts were assessed under the correct legal framework (while Patel blocks fact and credibility disputes). Under my pragmatic fairness lens, the better practical consequence is to police that boundary rigorously (dismissing disguised fact challenges) rather than to immunize genuine legal misapplications in a context where removal consequences are severe. I therefore remain with the Petitioner, while emphasizing that review must be narrow and should not permit reweighing or second-guessing discretionary judgment.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(D) expressly preserves jurisdiction over “constitutional claims or questions of law” notwithstanding § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i)’s limits, and Guerrero-Lasprilla held that “questions of law” include the application of a legal standard to undisputed or established facts (a mixed question). A hardship-eligibility determination under § 1229b(b)(1)(D), to the extent it challenges whether the agency correctly applied the “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” standard to settled facts, fits within that preserved category without opening the door to reweighing evidence or reviewing pure factual findings. Patel does not compel a contrary result because it addressed review of factual determinations underlying discretionary relief, whereas § 1252(a)(2)(D) still restores review for legal errors and mixed questions as defined in Guerrero-Lasprilla. A narrow ruling allowing review only for misapplication of the legal standard to established facts best respects Congress’s jurisdiction-stripping scheme while maintaining uniformity and institutional legitimacy by ensuring the agency follows the governing legal rule.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(D) restores jurisdiction for “constitutional claims or questions of law” notwithstanding § 1252(a)(2)(B), and that phrase is best read to include the application of a legal standard to established facts. Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr held that “questions of law” in § 1252(a)(2)(D) encompass such mixed questions, and nothing in § 1229b(b)(1)(D)’s hardship criterion justifies carving out an exception to that textual rule. Patel v. Garland confirms the statute draws a fact/law line—courts may not reweigh or revisit factfinding, but they may correct legal error in applying the hardship standard to the facts as found. Accordingly, courts may review whether the IJ/BIA misapplied the “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” standard to established facts while remaining barred from reviewing disputed factual determinations.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(D) restores review only for “constitutional claims or questions of law,” and the “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” inquiry under § 1229b is a highly fact-intensive, judgment-laden assessment that courts of appeals would inevitably reweigh if permitted to review it. Patel v. Garland interpreted § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i) broadly to bar review of factual determinations underlying cancellation and cautioned against using § 1252(a)(2)(D) to repackage fact disputes as legal questions, a concern that applies with special force to hardship determinations. Guerrero-Lasprilla’s recognition that some mixed questions can qualify as “questions of law” does not compel review here because hardship is not the kind of settled-facts/legal-standard application that can be reviewed without intruding on the agency’s discretionary, case-specific judgment. Practically, allowing review would expand appellate jurisdiction into routine cancellation disputes, undermining Congress’s evident aim to limit judicial second-guessing in this area and burdening immigration adjudication.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(D) restores jurisdiction for “questions of law” notwithstanding other jurisdiction-stripping provisions, and under Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr, that phrase includes mixed questions involving the application of a legal standard to established facts. The “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” eligibility determination under § 1229b is precisely that kind of application: accepting the IJ’s historical factfindings, a court can still review whether the agency applied the correct legal standard to those facts without reweighing evidence. Patel v. Garland confirms the statute draws a fact/law line—pure fact disputes remain unreviewable—but it does not permit categorically insulating legal misapplications simply because the inquiry is fact-intensive or arises in a discretionary-relief framework. Allowing review for legal error promotes uniformity and guards against unfairness in high-stakes cases affecting vulnerable families, while preserving agency primacy over factfinding and discretionary weighing.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(D) preserves jurisdiction over “questions of law” notwithstanding § 1252(a)(2)(B)’s jurisdiction-stripping, and in Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr we held that “questions of law” include mixed questions—i.e., the application of a legal standard to established facts. The “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” eligibility inquiry under § 1229b is precisely that kind of application: reviewing courts may assess whether the IJ/BIA applied the correct legal framework to the facts found, while still respecting the bar on reweighing evidence or revisiting factfinding. Patel v. Garland confirms the statute draws a fact/law line (foreclosing review of factual findings), but it does not retract Guerrero-Lasprilla’s rule that legal-standards-as-applied remain reviewable under § 1252(a)(2)(D). This reading promotes statutory coherence and administrable boundaries: courts review legal misapplications for uniformity, and the agency retains primacy over factual determinations and discretionary weighing.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(D) restores jurisdiction for “constitutional claims or questions of law” notwithstanding § 1252(a)(2)(B)’s jurisdiction-stripping, and the ordinary meaning of “questions of law” includes applying a legal standard to established facts. Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr held that “questions of law” in § 1252(a)(2)(D) encompasses mixed questions—i.e., whether settled facts satisfy a legal standard—and that reading controls here when a petitioner alleges the agency misapplied the “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” standard to undisputed facts under § 1229b. Patel v. Garland does not alter that conclusion because it addressed the unreviewability of factual findings and did not purport to retract Guerrero-Lasprilla’s interpretation of § 1252(a)(2)(D) for mixed questions. This approach respects Congress’s textually expressed compromise: courts may not reweigh facts or second-guess discretionary judgments, but they may correct legal errors in applying the hardship standard.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(D) preserves judicial review for “questions of law,” and in Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr this Court held that phrase includes mixed questions—“the application of a legal standard to undisputed or established facts.” The cancellation “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” eligibility inquiry, to the extent it challenges misapplication of that legal standard to established facts, fits within Guerrero-Lasprilla’s definition and therefore remains reviewable notwithstanding § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i). Patel v. Garland does not foreclose that conclusion because Patel addressed the nonreviewability of factual findings in discretionary-relief proceedings, not the reviewability of legal or mixed questions preserved by § 1252(a)(2)(D). Limiting review to genuine legal/mixed errors (and not fact reweighing) is also the most workable, precedent-respecting way to maintain uniformity while honoring Congress’s jurisdiction-stripping scheme.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(D) restores jurisdiction for “constitutional claims or questions of law” notwithstanding other jurisdiction-stripping provisions, and in Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr this Court held that “questions of law” includes the application of a legal standard to undisputed or established facts. Applying § 1229b(b)(1)(D)’s “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” standard to the facts found by the IJ/BIA is therefore a reviewable mixed question, so long as the court does not re-find facts or second-guess discretionary weighing. Patel v. Garland confirms that pure factual determinations remain barred from review, but it does not retract Guerrero-Lasprilla’s construction of § 1252(a)(2)(D) for mixed questions. Reading § 1252(a)(2)(D) to exclude hardship applications categorically would improperly narrow the statutory phrase “questions of law” as originally understood and as authoritatively construed by this Court.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(D) restores jurisdiction over “constitutional claims or questions of law” notwithstanding the INA’s broader jurisdiction-stripping provisions, and this Court has held that “questions of law” include the application of a legal standard to “undisputed or established facts.” Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr, 140 S. Ct. 1062, 1068–69 (2020). The cancellation-of-removal hardship requirement in § 1229b(b)(1)(D) supplies a legal standard (“exceptional and extremely unusual hardship”), and whether the agency correctly applied that standard to settled facts is therefore a reviewable mixed question under § 1252(a)(2)(D), even if courts remain barred from reweighing evidence or second-guessing discretionary judgments. Patel v. Garland, 142 S. Ct. 1614 (2022), does not compel a different result because it addresses the scope of review over factual determinations and discretionary relief, whereas this case concerns correcting legal misapplication to established facts—an essential procedural safeguard in high-stakes removal proceedings.
